An unpredictable, high-impact event that experts rationalize in hindsight. Nassim Taleb's term: before Australia, all swans were white by definition. 9/11, 2008 crash, COVID: obvious in retrospect, invisible in prospect. Our models exclude what matters most.
A brief recovery in a declining market — even a dead cat bounces if dropped from high enough. The sucker's rally that tricks optimists before the next leg down. The relief that isn't.

Hold On for Dear Life — originally a typo in a 2013 Bitcoin forum post, now crypto gospel. Don't panic sell; diamond hands through the crash. The strategy that works until it doesn't. Also retronymed: Hold On for Dear Life.
Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt — negative information spread to drive prices down. Originally IBM's competitive tactic. In crypto: any bearish news is dismissed as FUD. The tribal epistemology of markets.

The broker's demand for more collateral when leveraged positions move against you. Deposit more or get liquidated. The moment leverage reverses from amplifier to executioner. The phone call that ends careers.
When short sellers are forced to buy to cover positions, driving prices higher, forcing more covering. A feedback loop of pain. GameStop 2021: retail traders versus hedge funds, memes versus models.
Borrowing in low-interest currency, investing in high-interest currency — pocketing the spread. Works until the borrowed currency spikes. Picking up nickels in front of steamrollers. The widow-maker.

The graph of interest rates across maturities — normally slopes up (long-term rates higher than short). Inverted yield curve: short rates exceed long. The recession predictor with an imperfect but impressive track record.
When futures prices exceed spot prices — the normal state for commodities with storage costs. Rolling futures contracts in contango bleeds money. The silent killer of commodity ETFs.
When spot prices exceed futures prices — supply shortage, immediate demand. The opposite of contango. Rolling futures in backwardation generates positive roll yield. The rare favorable condition.

The ease of buying or selling without moving the price — cash is perfectly liquid; real estate isn't. Liquidity vanishes precisely when you need it. Everyone heads for the exit at once, and the door shrinks.

Using borrowed money to amplify returns — and losses. 10x leverage: 10% gain becomes 100%, 10% loss wipes you out. The tool that makes fortunes and destroys them. Every crisis has leverage at its heart.

Financial instruments whose value derives from underlying assets — options, futures, swaps. Used to hedge risk or to speculate with leverage. Warren Buffett: 'financial weapons of mass destruction.' Also: essential market infrastructure.
Valuing assets at current market prices rather than purchase price — honest but volatile. When markets freeze, there is no market to mark to. The accounting that turns paper losses into real ones.

When insurance against risk encourages risk-taking — banks that expect bailouts gamble bigger. The more protected you are from consequences, the more recklessly you act. Every safety net creates perverse incentives.

When one party has information the other lacks, and this distorts who participates — sick people buy health insurance, lemons get sold. Markets unravel when information asymmetry is severe. Akerlof's insight.

A state where no one can be made better off without making someone worse off — the economist's criterion of optimality. Says nothing about fairness: slavery could be Pareto efficient. Necessary but not sufficient.

Value destroyed by market distortions — the transactions that don't happen because of taxes, monopolies, or price controls. The area of the triangle economists love to draw. Inefficiency made geometric.

Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization — the profitability metric that ignores financing and accounting choices. Loved by private equity, mocked by Buffett: 'Does management think the tooth fairy pays for capital expenditures?'

The premium paid above book value in acquisitions — the accounting entry for overpaying. Supposedly represents brand value, synergies, intangibles. Often written down years later when the deal sours. The graveyard of M&A optimism.
Central bank buying assets to inject money into the economy — printing money with extra steps. QE1, QE2, QE∞. The policy that worked until it caused inflation. The monetary experiment of the 2010s.
Market panic when central banks hint at reducing stimulus — the 2013 bond selloff when Bernanke mentioned tapering. Addicts don't like hearing about withdrawal. The market's dependency exposed.
Trading ahead of client orders using inside knowledge — illegal for brokers, gray area for high-frequency traders who detect order flow. The parasitic extraction that erodes trust.
Artificially inflating an asset's price through misleading hype, then selling. The classic stock fraud, now endemic in crypto. The telegram group that makes insiders rich and followers poor.
Buying overpriced assets expecting to sell to someone even less informed — the logic of bubbles. You're not the fool if you sell first. Musical chairs with money. Works until the music stops.

Everything in its place — the chef's discipline of preparing and organizing all ingredients before cooking. Not just efficiency but mindset: the calm that comes from readiness. Chaos controlled through preparation.
Under vacuum — cooking food sealed in plastic at precise low temperatures for extended periods. Perfect doneness edge-to-edge. The technique that modernist cuisine mainstreamed. Patience as method.
terms.etymology: French: sous (under) + vide (vacuum)

terms.definition: Savory deliciousness — the fifth taste, beyond sweet, sour, salty, bitter. Glutamates in parmesan, soy sauce, tomatoes, mushrooms. Identified by Ikeda in 1908, dismissed by the West until recently. The taste that makes food satisfying.

The chemical browning that creates flavor — amino acids and sugars reacting under heat. Bread crust, seared steak, roasted coffee. Not caramelization (that's just sugar). The reaction that makes cooked food taste cooked.
To deglaze — adding liquid to a hot pan to dissolve the caramelized fond stuck to the bottom. Wine, stock, even water. The technique that turns brown bits into sauce. Waste not, want not.

Foundation — both the caramelized bits on the pan (fond de cuisson) and the stock base of sauces (fond de cuisine). French cooking builds layers: protein leaves fond, liquid captures it, sauce emerges. Architecture of flavor.

The five mother sauces of classical French cuisine — béchamel, velouté, espagnole, hollandaise, tomate. Escoffier's taxonomy: master these and derive hundreds of variations. The grammar of French cooking.
Matchstick cut — vegetables sliced into thin, uniform strips. Precision as technique. Along with brunoise, chiffonade, and others: the knife skills that separate amateur from professional.
Fine dice — vegetables cut into tiny 3mm cubes, often starting from julienne. The smallest standard cut. Uniformity ensures even cooking. The meditation of knife work.
Ribbon cut — leafy herbs or greens rolled and sliced into thin strips. Basil over pasta, lettuce as garnish. The elegant finish.
Water bath — cooking or warming via a container set in hot water. Gentle, indirect heat. For custards, chocolate, delicate sauces. Also: the steam table keeping brunch warm.
To blanch — briefly boiling then shocking in ice water. Sets color, removes bitterness, loosens skins, par-cooks. The technique that makes vegetables vibrant green.
Preserved by slow-cooking in fat — duck legs submerged in duck fat, garlic in oil. Pre-refrigeration preservation that happens to be delicious. The texture that falls off the bone.
terms.etymology: French: confire (to preserve)

terms.definition: To braise — searing then slow-cooking covered in liquid. Breaks down tough cuts into tender. The alchemy of time: collagen becomes gelatin, sinew becomes silk. Peasant cooking elevated to art.

A stable mixture of immiscible liquids — oil and water held together by lecithin or other emulsifiers. Mayonnaise, hollandaise, vinaigrette. The chemistry that makes sauces creamy. Break the emulsion: greasy disaster.
A beam anchored at only one end, projecting into space — Fallingwater's terraces, diving boards, balconies. The structural drama of defying gravity. Engineering as spectacle.
The arrangement of windows in a building — from Latin fenestra (window). The pattern that gives a façade rhythm. How light enters, how buildings breathe. The eyes of architecture.
The architectural style of raw concrete — béton brut. Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation, Boston City Hall. Loved by architects, loathed by the public, rediscovered by Instagram. Honesty as aesthetic.
terms.etymology: From French béton brut (raw concrete)

terms.definition: The German art school (1919-1933) that unified art, craft, and technology — Gropius, Mies, Kandinsky. Form follows function. The template for modernist design. The Nazis closed it; its ideas conquered the world.
terms.etymology: German: Bau (building) + Haus (house)

terms.definition: Columns that raise a building above ground — Le Corbusier's Five Points of Architecture. The building floats; the ground flows beneath. Freeing the plan from the earth.
A structural bracket projecting from a wall to support weight — the technique that built Gothic cathedrals and Medieval castles. Stone stepping out to catch stone. The medieval cantilever.
The external arched support that channels Gothic cathedral walls' outward thrust to the ground — engineering that enabled walls of glass. Structure made visible and beautiful.
The central organizing idea of an architectural design — the big move, the diagram, the concept from which all decisions flow. Not the whole solution but its seed.
The solid mass in architectural drawings shown as filled black — walls, structure, the space you can't occupy. The figure-ground relationship. What's not room is poché.
Intense final design sprint — from the cart (charrette) that collected student drawings at the École des Beaux-Arts. Now any deadline crunch. The all-nighter before presentation.

The mental discomfort of holding contradictory beliefs — the smoker who knows smoking kills. We resolve it by changing beliefs, adding rationalizations, or ignoring information. Festinger's discovery: the mind demands consistency.

The cognitive bias where incompetent people overestimate their ability while experts underestimate theirs — you need competence to recognize incompetence. The confidence of the ignorant. Mount Stupid before the valley of despair.

The tendency to seek and interpret information that confirms existing beliefs — we google to prove ourselves right, not to learn. The algorithm of self-reinforcement. The bias that makes all other biases sticky.

Over-relying on the first piece of information encountered — the initial price sets expectations, the first number frames negotiation. Arbitrary anchors affect judges, doctors, everyone. The power of going first.

Judging probability by how easily examples come to mind — plane crashes feel more common than car accidents because they're memorable. Vivid beats statistical. The news distorts reality by selecting the dramatic.

Continuing a losing course because of past investment — the movie is bad but you've paid for the ticket. Throwing good money after bad. The inability to write off what's already lost. Concorde fallacy.
Believing after the fact that you knew it all along — 'I knew the market would crash.' Memory rewrites itself. The obstacle to learning from mistakes. Everyone's a genius in hindsight.
Attributing others' behavior to character while attributing our own to circumstance — he's late because he's irresponsible; I'm late because of traffic. We're harsher judges of others than ourselves.

Letting one positive trait color perception of everything else — attractive people seem smarter, successful companies seem well-managed. The cognitive shortcut that distorts judgment. First impressions contaminate everything.
Giving up after repeated failure even when escape becomes possible — Seligman's dogs stopped trying. The psychological trap of depression and poverty. When trauma teaches that action is futile.

Manipulating someone into questioning their own reality — from the 1944 film where a husband dims gaslights while denying change. Psychological abuse through reality distortion. 'That never happened. You're crazy.'
Attributing your own unacceptable thoughts to others — the cheater who suspects cheating, the liar who trusts no one. Freudian defense mechanism. We see in others what we can't face in ourselves.
Redirecting feelings about one person onto another — the patient who falls in love with the therapist, seeing a parent. Freud's discovery, now therapeutic tool. The past animating the present.
Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities — aggression into sports, sexuality into art. The healthiest defense mechanism. Civilization built on redirected drives.

Learning through consequences — Skinner's rats pressing levers. Positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, punishment. The behaviorist mechanism beneath all training. Reward what you want; ignore what you don't.

The brain's ability to rewire itself — forming new connections, reassigning functions. The discovery that ended 'hardwired' pessimism. Stroke patients recover; meditators change structure. The brain as ongoing construction site.
Misrepresenting an argument to make it easier to attack — you argue against the caricature, not the position. The scarecrow you can knock down. Defeat an opponent who never showed up.
A distraction from the actual issue — the irrelevant point that derails debate. From training hunting dogs with smoked fish. Change the subject when you're losing.

You too — deflecting criticism by pointing to the accuser's hypocrisy. 'You criticize my emissions? You flew here.' The fallacy of avoiding substance through counter-accusation. Hypocrisy doesn't refute truth.

Claiming one step inevitably leads to extremes without justification — 'If we allow X, soon we'll have Y and Z.' Sometimes valid (precedent matters), often fallacious (steps are distinguishable). The paranoid argument.
Presenting only two options when more exist — 'You're with us or against us.' The excluded middle. Forcing a choice between extremes, ignoring nuance. Either/or thinking.

Assuming the conclusion in the premise — circular reasoning. 'God exists because the Bible says so, and the Bible is true because it's God's word.' The argument that proves nothing. Often misused to mean 'raises the question.'

Using an expert's opinion as proof — valid when the expert is relevant; fallacious when not. Einstein on physics versus Einstein on politics. Celebrity endorsements. The shortcut that sometimes works.
Assuming natural means good — arsenic is natural; vaccines aren't. The naturalistic fallacy. Evolution gave us cancer and cruelty. Nature is not a moral guide.
Aristotle's three modes of persuasion — ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion), logos (logic). The complete rhetorical arsenal. Most persuasion is pathos wearing logos costume, delivered by ethos.
The strongest version of an opponent's argument — the opposite of straw man. Engage the best case, not the worst. Intellectual honesty as practice. If you can't steelman it, you don't understand it.
Defending a controversial claim by retreating to an uncontroversial one — the bailey is the bold position; the motte is the defensible retreat. 'I just meant...' after pushback. Strategic ambiguity.
Overwhelming opponents with quantity of arguments, regardless of quality — named for creationist Duane Gish. Each claim takes seconds to make, minutes to refute. The firehose of falsehood.
Caused by medical treatment — the infection caught in hospital, the side effect worse than the disease. Medicine's dark side. First, do no harm is aspirational, not descriptive.
terms.etymology: Greek: iatros (healer) + genesis (origin)

terms.definition: Hospital-acquired — infections contracted during hospitalization. C. diff, MRSA, the bugs that breed where the sick gather. The paradox that hospitals can make you sicker.
terms.etymology: Greek: nosokomeion (hospital)

terms.definition: The study of causes — specifically, the cause of a disease. Unknown etiology: we don't know why this happens. The question before treatment: what went wrong?
terms.etymology: Greek: aitia (cause) + logos (study)

terms.definition: The predicted course of a disease — the forecast, the odds. Good prognosis: likely recovery. Poor prognosis: prepare affairs. The doctor's crystal ball, clouded by uncertainty.
terms.etymology: Greek: pro (before) + gnosis (knowledge)

terms.definition: The presence of multiple diseases simultaneously — diabetes and heart disease, depression and anxiety. Conditions cluster. Treatment complicates. The body doesn't respect diagnostic categories.
Treatment that relieves symptoms without curing — comfort care when cure fails. Pain management, quality of life. Not giving up but changing goals. The medicine of dignity.
terms.etymology: Latin: palliare (to cloak)

terms.definition: A treatment with no active ingredient that works anyway — the sugar pill that heals through belief. The placebo effect: 30-40% of drug efficacy. The mind-body problem made clinical.
terms.etymology: Latin: I shall please

terms.definition: Negative effects from expecting harm — the placebo's evil twin. Read the side effects and experience them. Voodoo death. Expectation shapes physiology.
terms.etymology: Latin: I shall harm

terms.definition: A sign or symptom so characteristic that it confirms diagnosis — Koplik's spots mean measles, no other tests needed. The diagnostic slam dunk. Rare in medicine; most symptoms are nonspecific.
Early symptoms before full disease — the aura before migraine, the fatigue before flu. The warning period. Sometimes actionable; often just ominous.
terms.etymology: Greek: pro (before) + dromos (running)

terms.definition: Of unknown cause — medicine's honest admission of ignorance. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: your lungs are scarring and we don't know why. The word that means 'we don't know.'
terms.etymology: Greek: idios (one's own) + pathos (suffering)

terms.definition: A condition resulting from a previous disease — the lung damage after COVID, the heart problems after rheumatic fever. The shadow the illness leaves. Recovery isn't always complete.

The smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning — /p/ and /b/ are different phonemes because 'pat' and 'bat' mean different things. The atoms of speech. Each language selects from the universal inventory.
The smallest unit of meaning — 'un-break-able' has three morphemes. Words decompose into meaningful pieces. The elements that combine into vocabulary.
How context shapes meaning — 'Nice weather we're having' during a storm. What's said versus what's meant. The study of implicature, speech acts, conversational norms. Language in use.
Words whose meaning depends on context — 'here,' 'now,' 'I,' 'this.' You can't interpret them without knowing who, where, when. The pointers that ground language in situation.
The rules governing sentence structure — word order, phrase structure, grammatical relations. Chomsky's domain. The difference between 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog.'
The study of meaning — what words and sentences mean, apart from how they're used. Truth conditions, reference, sense. 'That's just semantics' dismisses what actually matters.

Alternating between languages or dialects in conversation — switching to Spanish at home, professional English at work. Identity performed through linguistic choice. Everyone does it; bilinguals just do it more visibly.

A simplified language arising between groups with no common tongue — limited vocabulary, simplified grammar, used for trade. No native speakers. The makeshift bridge. If children grow up speaking it, it becomes a creole.
A pidgin that has become a native language — full complexity emerges in one generation. Haitian Creole, Tok Pisin. The proof that children don't just learn language; they create it.

A common language between speakers of different native tongues — originally the Mediterranean trade pidgin. Now English globally, Swahili in East Africa, Indonesian in its archipelago. The bridge language.
A word that appears only once in a corpus — occurring once in Shakespeare, once in the Bible. The translator's nightmare: context can't help. The lonely word.
A loan translation — borrowing a foreign expression by translating its parts. 'Skyscraper' becomes gratte-ciel (French), rascacielos (Spanish). The idea crosses; the sounds don't.
Words in different languages descended from the same ancestor — 'mother,' 'mater,' 'Mutter,' 'mère.' Shared heritage across millennia. The family resemblance that traces migrations.
Words that look similar across languages but differ in meaning — 'embarazada' (Spanish: pregnant) is not 'embarrassed.' The cognate that betrays. The translator's trap.
The right-hand side of a ship when facing forward. From Old English 'steorbord' (steering side), as the steering oar was traditionally mounted on the right.
terms.etymology: Old English steorbord

terms.definition: The left-hand side of a ship when facing forward. Originally 'larboard', changed to 'port' to avoid confusion with 'starboard' in verbal commands.
terms.etymology: From the loading port on the left side

terms.definition: A unit of length equal to six feet, used to measure water depth. Also means to understand deeply—to 'sound the depths' of a problem.
terms.etymology: Old English fæthm (outstretched arms)

terms.definition: The sideways drift of a ship downwind from its course. Metaphorically, the margin of freedom or flexibility in a situation.
terms.etymology: From lee (shelter from wind) + way

terms.definition: Shipboard gossip or rumors. Originally the cask of drinking water around which sailors would gather and chat—the ship's water cooler.
terms.etymology: From scuttle (hatch) + butt (cask)

terms.definition: A belt of calm winds near the equator where sailing ships could be stranded for weeks. Metaphorically, a state of stagnation or depression.
terms.etymology: Perhaps from Old English dol (dull)

terms.definition: A powerful whirlpool. From a specific tidal current off Norway's coast. Now denotes any turbulent, chaotic, or overwhelming situation.
terms.etymology: Dutch malen (to grind) + stroom (stream)

terms.definition: The adjustment of space between individual letter pairs to achieve visually pleasing spacing. Poor kerning creates awkward gaps or collisions.
The vertical space between lines of text, measured from baseline to baseline. Named for the thin strips of lead placed between lines of metal type.
terms.etymology: From lead strips in letterpress

terms.definition: Two or more letters combined into a single glyph, such as fi, fl, or æ. Originally a practical solution to letters that collided in metal type.
A statement at the end of a book giving details of its production—printer, typeface, paper. From ancient Greek practice of noting the scribe's name.
terms.etymology: Greek kolophōn (summit, finishing touch)

terms.definition: Books printed before 1501, during the infancy of printing. The term evokes swaddling clothes—these are books from when print was in its cradle.
terms.etymology: Latin incunabula (swaddling clothes, cradle)

terms.definition: Recto: the front (right-hand) page of a book. Verso: the back (left-hand) page. From the Latin for 'right' and 'turned'.
The inner margin of a book page, near the binding. Must be wide enough for comfortable reading without cracking the spine.
A widow is a lone line at the top of a page. An orphan is a lone line at the bottom. Both are considered typographic sins—no line should be left alone.
A vineyard or group of vineyards recognized for quality, especially in Burgundy and Bordeaux. Grand cru denotes the highest classification.
A legally defined geographic region for wine production, guaranteeing origin and often production methods. The terroir made official.
A trained wine professional, typically in a restaurant, who specializes in wine service and food pairing. From Old French for 'pack animal driver'.
Naturally occurring polyphenols in grape skins, seeds, and oak barrels that create astringency and structure in wine. The 'grip' you feel.
The complex aromas that develop in wine through aging, as opposed to primary fruit aromas. A mature wine's olfactory signature.
The streaks of wine that run down the inside of a glass after swirling. Indicates alcohol and glycerol content, not quality despite the myth.
A bending of the knees with the back held straight. The foundation of ballet technique, used to warm up and as preparation for jumps.
Rising to the balls of the feet or full pointe. From French 'raised'—the dancer lifts against gravity.
A dance for two, typically a ballerina and male partner, showcasing both virtuosity and partnership. The romantic centerpiece of classical ballet.
A pose on one leg with the other extended behind. Named for its resemblance to Arabic decorative patterns—a body made ornamental.
A turn in which the working leg whips around to provide momentum. The 32 fouettés in Swan Lake are a legendary test of technique.
Dancing on the tips of the toes in reinforced shoes. The ethereal, gravity-defying image of ballet—achieved through years of training and pain.
The horizontal rail used for support during ballet warm-up exercises. Every ballet class begins at the barre before moving to center work.
The art of dramatic composition and theatrical representation. A dramaturg researches, advises on text, and bridges playwright and production.
The final resolution of a plot's complications. From French 'unknotting'—the moment when all threads are untangled.
A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud while alone on stage. The audience becomes privy to the inner mind.
terms.etymology: Latin solus (alone) + loqui (to speak)

terms.definition: A remark spoken to the audience that other characters supposedly cannot hear. A theatrical conspiracy between actor and viewer.
The imaginary barrier between performers and audience. 'Breaking' it means directly acknowledging the audience—shattering the illusion.
The precise staging of actors' movements and positions. Where you stand, when you move—the choreography of drama.
The backstage room where performers wait before going on stage. Origin disputed—possibly from green baize fabric or nervous pallor.
The formal description of a coat of arms in heraldic language. A precise technical vocabulary that can recreate any design from text alone.
The heraldic term for silver or white. One of the two 'metals' in heraldry, along with or (gold).
The heraldic term for red. From Old French goules (red fur neckpieces). One of the five traditional 'colours'.
The left side of a shield (from the bearer's perspective, right from viewer's). Latin for 'left'—hence the word's ominous connotations.
An animal lying down with head raised, alert. Contrasts with dormant (sleeping) and passant (walking).
An animal rearing up on its hind legs in profile, forepaws raised. The most aggressive heraldic posture—lions rampant are ubiquitous.
Islamic philosophy derived from Greek thought. Practiced by Al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Averroes, it sought to reconcile reason with revelation.
Scholarly consensus in Islamic law. When qualified jurists agree on a ruling, it becomes binding—collective wisdom as legal source.
Wisdom in Arabic philosophy. Not mere knowledge but deep understanding—the practical application of truth to life.
Islamic scholastic theology. Literally 'speech'—the discipline of defending religious doctrines through rational argument.
An isthmus or barrier between two things—in Islamic thought, the realm between death and resurrection. A liminal spiritual space.
A poetic form of rhyming couplets with a refrain, traditionally about love and loss. Each couplet is self-contained yet part of a whole.
A four-line poem with AABA rhyme scheme. Omar Khayyam's Rubaiyat made the form famous in the West.
A poem of rhyming couplets, often of epic length. Rumi's Masnavi-ye-Ma'navi is the supreme example—26,000 verses of mystical teaching.
A word or phrase repeated at the end of each couplet in a ghazal, following the rhyme. Creates hypnotic musicality.
A poet's pen name, traditionally inserted in the final couplet. The poet signs their work within the poem itself.
A collected volume of a poet's work, arranged alphabetically by the last letter of the rhyme. The standard format for Persian poetry anthologies.
A melodic framework for improvisation, with specific ascending/descending patterns, characteristic phrases, and emotional associations (rasa).
A rhythmic cycle that provides the temporal framework for composition and improvisation. Cycles range from 3 to 128 beats.
The smallest interval of pitch recognized in Indian music—22 shrutis per octave versus Western music's 12 semitones.
Ornamental techniques including oscillations, slides, and grace notes that give Indian classical music its distinctive expressiveness.
The slow, meditative, rhythm-free opening of a raga performance. The musician gradually reveals the raga's character, note by note.
A duet between two soloists, often playing different instruments. Competitive yet collaborative—musical dialogue and friendly combat.
A lineage or school of musicians passing down distinctive style through generations. Literally 'household'—musical knowledge as family inheritance.
The formless base of all matter in alchemy. Everything begins as and can be reduced to this primordial substance—chaos before creation.
The first stage of the alchemical work—blackening, putrefaction, death. Jung interpreted it as confronting the shadow self.
The second stage—whitening, purification, washing away impurities. Psychologically, the emergence of insight from darkness.
The final stage—reddening, the achievement of the philosopher's stone. Symbolizes wholeness, integration, spiritual gold.
The 'Great Work'—the alchemical process of creating the philosopher's stone. Now means any artist's or thinker's masterpiece.
A serpent eating its own tail, symbolizing eternal cyclic renewal. What begins ends where it started—destruction feeding creation.
'Dissolve and coagulate'—the essential alchemical operation. Break down to build up. Destruction precedes creation.
A choreographed pattern of movements encoding combat techniques. The living textbook of a martial art, passed down through bodies.
The focus of physical and mental energy at the moment of impact. The explosive concentration that makes a technique decisive.
Continued awareness and alertness after a technique. The fight isn't over when you think it is—maintain readiness.
A sharp exhalation or shout focusing energy and spirit at the moment of action. The sound of ki (vital energy) being released.
A training hall for martial arts. Literally 'place of the way'—the physical space where the path is practiced.
Teacher or master. Literally 'one who came before'—someone who walks the path ahead of you and shows the way.
A rank indicating proficiency level, typically starting after achieving black belt. The dan ranks represent deepening mastery.
Toward the stern of a ship, behind. 'Abaft the beam' means behind an imaginary line across the ship's middle.
At right angles to the ship's length. A landmark 'abeam' is directly to the side, neither ahead nor behind.
A command to stop or cease. From Dutch 'houd vast' (hold fast). The sailor's imperative halt.
terms.etymology: Dutch houd vast

terms.definition: To secure a ship's hatches with strips of wood (battens) before a storm. Now means to prepare for any difficulty.
To secure a rope by winding it around a cleat or pin. Also a command to disregard a previous order.
The lowest internal part of a ship's hull where water collects. Bilge water is notoriously foul—hence 'bilge' as nonsense.
The stand housing the ship's compass, with correcting magnets and a light for night navigation. The navigator's altar.
A short thick post on a ship or wharf for securing mooring lines. The humble anchor point of enormous vessels.
Boatswain—the petty officer responsible for a ship's deck crew, rigging, and anchors. Pronounced 'BOH-sun'.
A spar extending forward from the bow, carrying forestays and sails. The ship's pointing finger.
A wall-like partition dividing a ship's interior into compartments. Critical for containing flooding and fire.
A vertical rotating machine for winding rope or chain, used for raising anchors. Sailors pushed its bars in endless circles.
Tilting a ship on its side to clean or repair the hull below the waterline. A vulnerable position—hence 'careening out of control'.
A beam projecting from the bow for raising and carrying the anchor. Named for the carved cat faces that often decorated them.
Sealing the seams between planks with oakum and pitch to make the hull watertight. An ancient shipwright's art.
A T-shaped fitting for securing ropes. Simple, elegant, essential—the grammar of the working deck.
A raised border around a hatch or cockpit to prevent water from entering. The ship's lips.
A stairway or ladder leading from the deck to the cabin below. The threshold between above and below.
Navigation by calculating position from speed, time, and course—without celestial observation. Deduced reckoning, corrupted to 'dead'.
The depth of water a ship needs to float. A ship 'draws' this much water. Deep draft limits where you can go.
A fitting that guides a rope, changing its direction without chafing. Invisible when working, obvious when absent.
A carved figure at the ship's prow. Once believed to appease sea gods; now means a leader without real power.
Wreckage floating after a shipwreck. Legally distinct from jetsam (thrown overboard intentionally). The sea's detritus.
Cargo deliberately thrown overboard to lighten a ship in distress. What we sacrifice to survive.
Forecastle—the forward part of a ship where crew quarters are located. Pronounced 'FOKE-sul'. Where sailors lived.
The distance from waterline to deck. More freeboard means a drier, safer ship; less means more cargo but more risk.
To roll and secure a sail to its yard or boom. The opposite of setting sail—putting the ship to sleep.
A ship's kitchen. Compact, efficient, rolling with the sea. The cook works in a space where nothing stays still.
A passage or ramp for boarding a ship. Also an order to clear the way—make a path!
The upper edge of a ship's side. Pronounced 'GUNN-ul'. Originally reinforced to support guns.
A rope for raising and lowering sails or flags. From 'haul yard'—pull the yard (the horizontal spar).
A thick rope or cable for mooring or towing. The heavy-duty lines that hold great ships to the shore.
To stop a sailing vessel by backing some sails while keeping others set. The ship drifts slowly, riding out a storm.
To move a ship by dropping a small anchor ahead and winching toward it. Laborious progress when wind fails.
The central structural beam running the length of the hull's bottom. The ship's spine. 'On an even keel' means balanced.
One nautical mile per hour. Measured by counting knots on a line paid out behind the ship—hence the name.
A short rope for securing or fastening. Now any cord worn around the neck—the sailor's reach extended to land.
The side sheltered from the wind. 'In the lee of' means protected by. The safe side of any obstacle.
A ship's tilt to one side from uneven loading or damage. Not rolling (temporary) but listing (persistent imbalance).
The official record of a ship's voyage. Named for the log thrown overboard to measure speed. Every captain's diary.
The arrangement by which a ship is secured in place—anchors, lines, buoys. A ship at rest is still held by many forces.
Markings on a ship's hull showing maximum safe loading depths for different water conditions. Samuel Plimsoll's lifesaving reform.
Rope rungs tied between shrouds, forming a ladder to climb the mast. Pronounced 'RAT-lins'. The sailor's stairway to heaven.
The system of ropes, cables, and chains supporting masts and controlling sails. Standing rigging stays; running rigging moves.
An opening in the ship's side to drain water from the deck. Also slang for to sink or ruin—scupper a plan.
A rope controlling a sail's angle to the wind. Not the sail itself—that's a common landlubber error.
Standing rigging that supports the mast from the sides. The mast's guy-wires, keeping it upright against the wind's push.
Measuring water depth with a weighted line. The leadsman's call—'by the mark, twain'—named Mark Twain.
To join ropes by interweaving their strands. 'Splice the mainbrace' meant an extra rum ration—celebration.
A large balloon-like sail used when running before the wind. Colorful and dramatic—the sail of speed and spectacle.
A strong rope supporting the mast from fore or aft. The forestay runs to the bow; the backstay to the stern.
The rear of the ship. Opposite of bow. Where the name is painted and the rudder hangs.
A continuous line of planking running the length of the hull. Ships are built strake by strake, plank over plank.
To turn the bow through the wind to change course. Also the course itself—on the port tack, on the starboard tack.
A seat across a boat, also serving as structural bracing. To sit athwart is to sit crosswise.
The sides of the hull above the waterline. What you paint, what people see, what takes the weather.
The flat surface at the stern. The ship's back wall—where the name is mounted, where the dinghy hangs.
The fore-and-aft balance of a ship in the water. Down by the bow or down by the stern—both problematic.
To raise the anchor preparatory to sailing. The moment of commitment—once weighed, you're going somewhere.
A horizontal rotating machine for raising the anchor. The capstan's horizontal cousin.
The outer end of a yard (horizontal spar). 'Sun over the yardarm' meant noon—time for the first drink.
The part of a lowercase letter extending above the x-height: b, d, f, h, k, l. Reaching upward.
The part of a lowercase letter extending below the baseline: g, j, p, q, y. Reaching downward.
The height of lowercase letters without ascenders or descenders—measured by 'x'. Determines a typeface's apparent size.
The invisible line on which letters sit. Most characters rest here; descenders drop below it.
The small projecting feature at the end of letter strokes. Times New Roman has serifs; Helvetica doesn't.
A typeface without serifs—clean, modern, geometric. 'Sans' is French for 'without'.
The enclosed or partially enclosed space within a letter: the hole in 'o', the bowl of 'a'.
The curved part of a letter enclosing a counter: the round part of 'b', 'd', 'p', 'o'.
The main vertical stroke of a letter. The backbone of 'l', the uprights of 'H'.
A horizontal stroke connecting two stems, as in 'H' and 'A'. Also called a bar.
The tapered or curved end of a stroke that doesn't terminate in a serif. The elegant finishing touch.
An ornamental extension or flourish on a letter. Decorative swashes add calligraphic flair to type.
The end of a stroke that doesn't have a serif. Ball terminals are rounded; beak terminals are pointed.
The point where two strokes meet at the top of a letter, as in 'A'. The typographic peak.
The point where two strokes meet at the bottom of a letter, as in 'V'. The typographic valley.
The interior angle where two strokes meet, as inside the 'V'. The apex seen from inside.
The curved stroke of 'h', 'm', 'n' connecting the stem to the arch.
The main curved stroke of 'S'. The letter's sinuous backbone.
A small projection from a main stroke, smaller than a serif. An accent of attitude.
The descending stroke of 'Q', 'R', or 'K'. The letter's signature flourish.
The small stroke projecting from the top of lowercase 'g'. Not all g's have ears.
The stroke connecting the two bowls of a double-story 'g'.
The lower bowl of a double-story 'g'. Some typefaces have open loops; others closed.
The downward diagonal stroke of 'K', 'R', and 'k'. Not quite a tail, not quite a stem.
A horizontal stroke that doesn't connect on one or both ends: the top of 'T', the strokes of 'E'.
The uniform adjustment of space between all characters in a block of text. Looser or tighter overall.
A unit equal to the current point size. An em-dash is one em wide. Named for the width of 'M' in metal type.
Half an em. An en-dash is used for ranges (1990–2000). Named for the width of 'N'.
A unit of type measurement equal to 12 points, or about 1/6 inch. The inch of typography.
The smallest unit of type measurement—approximately 1/72 inch. 12 points make a pica.
A page number, or a sheet folded once to make two leaves (four pages). From Latin 'leaf'.
A left-hand page in a book (even-numbered). The back of a leaf. Opposite of recto.
A right-hand page in a book (odd-numbered). The front of a leaf. Where chapters traditionally begin.
A folded sheet forming a section of a book, typically 8, 16, or 32 pages. Books are bound signature by signature.
The arrangement of pages on a press sheet so they'll be in order when folded. The printer's spatial puzzle.
When a printed element extends beyond the trim edge. The image 'bleeds' off the page—no white margin.
The final cut size of a printed piece. What remains after the edges are cut away.
In hot metal, a line of type cast as a single piece. Also the space for running headers/footers.
The width of a column of text, usually in picas. Ideal measure: 45-75 characters for comfortable reading.
The uneven edge of a column of text set flush left or right. A good rag has gentle, not jagged, undulation.
Distracting vertical gaps in text caused by word spaces aligning across multiple lines. A sign of bad justification.
A single word or short line at the end of a paragraph. Left behind, looking lonely.
Setting punctuation slightly outside the text margin for optical alignment. The margin looks straighter.
Capital letters drawn at roughly x-height. Used for acronyms, abbreviations, and elegant headers.
Numerals with varying heights—some ascending, some descending—that blend with lowercase text. Also called text figures.
Numerals of uniform height, aligning with capitals. Modern and tabular, but can look clunky in running text.
An ornamental character or symbol—bullets, stars, pointing hands. The typographer's garnish.
A typographic ornament resembling a flower or leaf. Used to decorate or separate text. The printer's flower.
The paragraph symbol: ¶. From Greek 'paragraphos'. Once marked new paragraphs before indentation became standard.
A pointing hand symbol: ☞. Used in margins to draw attention. From Latin 'little hand'. Also called a fist.
The first word of the next page printed at the bottom of the current page. Helped binders order loose sheets.
Text printed in red, especially headings or initial letters. From Latin 'ruber' (red). Now means any set of instructions.
The metal frame that holds type and blocks for letterpress printing. The forme goes in the chase.
The assembled type and blocks locked in a chase, ready for printing. What goes on the press.
Expandable wedges that lock type in the chase. Pronounced 'coin'. The pressure that holds it all together.
Blocks of wood or metal used to fill blank spaces in a forme. What isn't type is furniture.
A thin strip of wood used for spacing in letterpress. Smaller than furniture, larger than leading.
Individual pieces of type. To be 'out of sorts' meant lacking specific characters—hence the modern idiom for feeling unwell.
A hand-held adjustable tray for assembling type character by character. The compositor's instrument.
A drawer with compartments for storing type. Capital letters were in the upper case; small letters in the lower case.
The complete armorial display: shield, helmet, crest, mantling, supporters, motto. The full heraldic statement.
The shield on which arms are displayed. The heraldic canvas. Also a small shield within a larger one.
The background of a shield, before any charges are placed. The tincture of the field is named first in a blazon.
Any emblem or figure placed on the field of a shield. Lions, eagles, crosses, crescents—all are charges.
A basic geometric charge: fess (horizontal bar), pale (vertical bar), bend (diagonal), chief (top third).
A horizontal band across the middle of the shield, typically one-third its height. A fundamental ordinary.
A vertical band down the center of the shield. The fess turned sideways.
A diagonal band from upper dexter to lower sinister. A bend sinister goes the other way—not illegitimacy, despite the myth.
The upper third of the shield, treated as a charge. 'In chief' means in this top section.
An inverted V-shaped ordinary. Represents rafters of a house—hence association with builders and protection.
A diagonal cross, like an X. St. Andrew's cross. The Scottish flag is a white saltire on blue.
A vertical and horizontal band intersecting at the center. Hundreds of variant crosses exist in heraldry.
A border around the edge of the shield. Often used to mark cadency—a difference between family branches.
A small square in the upper dexter corner of the shield. Often bears a secondary emblem.
One fourth of a shield, when divided by a cross. Quartering combines arms from different lineages.
The colors used in heraldry. Metals (or, argent), colours (gules, azure, vert, sable, purpure), and furs.
Gold in heraldry, typically depicted as yellow. One of the two metals. From French/Latin for gold.
Blue in heraldry. From the Arabic for lapis lazuli. One of the five traditional colours.
Green in heraldry. From French for green. Relatively rare as a field color.
Black in heraldry. Named for the black fur of the sable animal.
Purple in heraldry. The rarest of the traditional colours, as purple dye was historically expensive.
A fur pattern: black spots on white, representing ermine winter pelts. Symbol of royalty and nobility.
A fur pattern of alternating blue and white shield-shapes, representing squirrel pelts. Cinderella's slippers may have been vair, not 'verre' (glass).
The right side of a shield from the bearer's viewpoint (left as you look at it). The more honorable side.
An animal walking, three paws on the ground, one forepaw raised. The typical posture of the English lions.
An animal standing with all four feet on the ground. Alert but not in motion.
An animal sitting on its haunches, forepaws on the ground. Lions sejant are less common than rampant.
An animal looking backward over its shoulder. Added to any posture—'passant regardant', 'rampant regardant'.
An animal looking outward at the viewer. The English royal lions are 'passant guardant'.
A bird shown with wings spread and tips upward. The imperial eagle is always displayed.
A fish swimming horizontally across the shield.
A fish swimming vertically, head upward, as if rising to breathe.
The system of marks distinguishing junior branches of a family. Labels, crescents, mullets—each child's difference.
A horizontal bar with hanging points, mark of the eldest son during his father's lifetime.
A star, typically five-pointed, representing a spur rowel. Mark of the third son.
A half-moon with horns pointing upward. Mark of the second son.
A bird without feet, representing a swift or martin. Mark of the fourth son.
A ring. Mark of the fifth son.
Cloth draped from the helmet, often shown slashed and flowing. Originally protected armor from sun and rain.
A figure mounted on top of the helmet. Not the coat of arms itself—a common error.
A twisted roll of fabric between crest and helmet, in the principal colors. Also called a wreath.
Figures standing on either side of the shield, appearing to hold it up. Usually reserved for high nobility.
The base on which supporters stand—often a mound, waves, or symbolic ground.
A short phrase on a scroll, usually beneath the shield. War cries, moral principles, family sentiments.
Combining two coats of arms side by side on one shield, typically for marriage. Each squeezed to fit.
The arrangement of multiple coats of arms on a single shield, showing lineage and alliances.
A Roman military standard—a cloth square hung from a crossbar. The ancestor of modern flags. Gives vexillology its name.
The upper corner of a flag, typically the hoist side. The U.S. stars occupy the canton.
The half of the flag farthest from the pole—the part that flies free. Also the flag's horizontal length.
The half of the flag nearest the pole. Also the flag's vertical width. You hoist a flag up the pole.
The background color or pattern of a flag. The French field is three vertical stripes; Japan's is white.
Any emblem or device on a flag. Stars, crescents, eagles, symbols—all are charges.
A narrow border separating two colors that would otherwise touch improperly. The white stripes in the Union Jack are fimbriations.
A flag of three horizontal or vertical stripes. France, Germany, Italy, Russia—tribands dominate world flags.
A three-colored flag, specifically vertical stripes. The French tricolore sparked a revolution in flag design.
A two-colored flag divided horizontally or vertically. Poland, Monaco, Ukraine.
An off-center cross extending to the flag's edges, shifted toward the hoist. Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland, Iceland.
A zigzag or triangular edge between flag sections. Bahrain's and Qatar's flags have serrated divisions.
A flag with a V-shaped cut in the fly, creating two points. Common in Scandinavian naval ensigns.
A triangular or swallowtail flag, typically identifying a yacht club. A sailor's affiliation.
A small flag carried by military units, often swallow-tailed. The unit's identity in battle.
A long, narrow, tapering flag. Naval signal flags are often pennants.
A banner hung from a crossbar, often with streamers. Medieval Italian city-states carried gonfalons.
A flag indicating nationality, especially flown by ships. The Red, White, and Blue Ensigns of Britain.
A small flag flown at the bow of a warship. The Union Jack is Britain's naval jack.
A flag with the arms or badge of a sovereign or noble. Also a ceremonial or military flag.
A square or vertical flag bearing arms or emblems. Heraldic banners show the full coat of arms.
A national flag for use by civilians. Some nations have different civil and state flags.
A national flag for government use, sometimes with additional emblems. Austria's state flag adds an eagle.
A variant flown by the military or in time of war. Often more elaborate than the civil flag.
A foreign nation's flag flown by a visiting ship as a sign of respect. Maritime diplomacy.
A flag flown below the peak of the pole as a sign of mourning. Leaving room for the invisible flag of death.
To lower a flag briefly as a salute to another ship or dignitary. The U.S. flag is never dipped.
A distinctive part of a flag symbolizing unity—often in the canton. The stars in the U.S. flag form the union.
The material from which flags are made, or festive decorations of flag-like strips. Dressed overall in bunting.
A couplet—the basic unit of Persian poetry. Literally 'house'; each couplet is a complete dwelling of meaning.
A single line of poetry—half a couplet. The first misra sets up; the second completes.
The opening couplet of a ghazal, where both lines rhyme, establishing the pattern.
The final couplet of a ghazal, where the poet traditionally includes their pen name.
The rhyme in a ghazal—the sound that ends each couplet. Must remain consistent throughout.
A meter or rhythmic pattern. From Arabic 'sea'—the vast ocean of possible rhythms.
The science of prosody—the rules governing meter in Persian and Arabic poetry. The mathematics of verse.
A long monorhyme poem, often praising a patron. The formal ode of Persian literature.
An elegy or lamentation, especially for the martyrs of Karbala. Poetry as mourning.
A poem with short phrases added to each line, creating an echo effect. Augmented verse.
A poem where stanzas are linked by a recurring refrain. The refrain ties disparate thoughts together.
Like tarji-band but with varying refrains. Each refrain unique, yet binding the stanzas.
A quatrain with AABA rhyme. Omar Khayyam's chosen form. Four lines to capture one truth.
A folk quatrain, simpler than the literary robai. Popular verse in rustic Persian.
Divine or passionate love—the central theme of Persian poetry. Not mere romance but spiritual longing.
Separation from the beloved. The pain that fuels the ghazal. Union is brief; separation is poetry.
Union with the beloved. The goal the poet rarely reaches. The silence after the poem.
Wine—literal intoxication or metaphor for divine ecstasy. The poet's sacrament.
The cupbearer who pours wine. Often addressed by the poet. Human server or divine intermediary.
The tavern or ruin where mystics gather. A place outside social norms, where truth is spoken.
A libertine mystic who defies convention. The antinomian spiritual seeker. Hafiz's persona.
An ascetic or pious hypocrite—the rind's opposite. Often mocked for outer piety without inner truth.
The beloved's curling lock of hair. A snare, a chain, a source of madness. The soul trapped in beauty.
The beauty spot or mole on the beloved's face. A dot that anchors the lover's obsession.
The beloved's lip. Source of words, kisses, the water of life. Ruby lips, life-giving lips.
The universal solvent sought by alchemists. Also the life-force or Mercury. The alpha and omega combined.
The alchemical furnace, designed to maintain constant heat. From Arabic for 'oven'. The alchemist's womb.
terms.etymology: Arabic al-tannur (oven)

terms.definition: Heating a substance until reduced to powder or ash. The first operation. Burning away what is not essential.
Dissolving the calcined matter in water or acid. The second operation. What was solid becomes fluid.
Isolating the components of dissolution. The third operation. Sorting what is pure from what is waste.
Recombining the purified elements. The fourth operation. The chemical marriage.
Introduction of new life into the conjunction. The fifth operation. The substance begins to live.
Boiling and condensing to purify. The sixth operation. Rising and falling, ever more refined.
The final solidification of the purified matter. The seventh operation. The stone achieved.
The yellowing stage, sometimes placed between albedo and rubedo. The dawn before full illumination.
The 'peacock's tail'—a display of iridescent colors signaling transition in the work. Beauty mid-transformation.
Not common mercury but the volatile, spiritual principle in all matter. The soul that transforms.
The fixed, fiery principle. Soul as opposed to Mercury's spirit. What gives matter its individuality.
The third principle—body, materiality, the crystallizing force. What makes things solid.
The hermaphroditic figure representing the union of opposites. From 'res bina' (double thing). Completion in duality.
An acronym: 'Visita Interiora Terrae Rectificando Invenies Occultum Lapidem'—Visit the interior of the earth; by rectifying you will find the hidden stone.
The alchemical method of separating and recombining. From Greek 'to tear apart' and 'to gather'. Analysis and synthesis.
terms.etymology: Greek spao (tear) + ageiro (gather)

terms.definition: An essence capable of transmuting base metals. Also a spiritual quality that transforms what it touches.
A liquid form of the philosopher's stone, capable of healing and prolonging life. From Arabic 'al-iksir'.
terms.etymology: Arabic al-iksir

terms.definition: The fifth essence—beyond earth, water, fire, air. The pure, unchanging substance of heavenly bodies.
Increasing the quantity or potency of the philosopher's stone. The stone can make more of itself.
An airtight closure preventing escape of volatile spirits. Named for Hermes. Now 'hermetically sealed'.
A gourd-shaped vessel for distillation—the lower part that holds the liquid. From Latin for gourd.
The still's cap that collects and directs vapor. From Arabic 'al-anbiq'. The distillation apparatus.
terms.etymology: Arabic al-anbiq

terms.definition: A vessel with a long bent neck for distillation. The alchemist's curved thinking.
A circulatory vessel with tubes returning distillate to the body. Named for the bird that feeds its young from its breast.
Maria the Jewess—legendary founder of Western alchemy. Invented the bain-marie, tribikos, and kerotakis.
Thrice-great Hermes—mythical author of the Hermetic texts. Fusion of Greek Hermes and Egyptian Thoth.
The foundational alchemical text, attributed to Hermes. 'As above, so below.' The microcosm mirrors the macrocosm.
The philosopher's stone. Goal of the great work. Transmutes lead to gold, grants immortality, perfects the soul.
The transmutation of base metals into gold. From Greek 'gold-making'. The alchemist's most famous aim.
Drinkable gold—a liquid medicine containing gold. Believed to cure all ailments and extend life.
